flashcards.answer: Formation taxi procedures ensure safe, standardized ground movement of multiple aircraft. Lead directs coordination and communications, while Wing maintains safe spacing and monitors Lead while completing checklist items.
A section takeoff is when both aircraft maintain formation integrity and position through the entire takeoff roll. It develops confidence and skill in holding formation during critical flight phases.
A maneuver used to trade formation positions. Lead directs the change with a signal or radio call, and Wing assumes Lead responsibilities while the former Lead transitions to Wing.

A looser variation of parade formation allowing Wing more flexibility for checks, clearing, or relaxation. Commonly used during in-flight checks or frequency changes, cruise formation reduces Wing fatigue while maintaining formation integrity.

The crossunder repositions the Wing aircraft to the opposite side of Lead for clearing, sun angle, pattern entry, or maneuver setup. It requires precise, smooth control due to close proximity to Lead.

An interval takeoff uses timing separation between aircraft brake releases to create safe spacing for takeoff when a section takeoff is hazardous. Aircraft depart individually, then rendezvous in parade formation.

Parade formation is the foundation of formation flying. It emphasizes precise positioning, smooth control, and disciplined monitoring of Lead. Most formation training focuses on mastering Wing parade formation.

flashcards.answer:
(2W/2C/5N)
C - Illumination of the OBOGS TEMP message indicates a failure of the OBOGS heat exchanger, and is considered a failure of the
OBOGS system.
W - Emergency oxygen bottle provides approximately 10 minutes of oxygen. If aircraft pressure altitude is above 10,000 feet MSL, ensure the aircraft reaches an altitude of 10,000 feet MSL or lower prior to exhaustion of the emergency oxygen supply or the effects of hypoxia may incapacitate the crew.
W - The OBOGS concentrator may malfunction resulting in zeolite dust in the breathing system without an illumination of the OBOGS FAIL light. Indications of this malfunction include respiratory irritation, coughing, or the presence of white dust in the oxygen mask. Inhalation of zeolite dust should be avoided.
C - When breathing oxygen under increased pressure, breathe at a rate and depth slightly less than normal to preclude hyperventilation.
N - If physiological symptoms are recognized, immediate access to a pure and secure source of oxygen is the best course of action to expedite recovery. If the cockpit altitude is above 10,000 feet, pulling the GREEN RING is required since ambient cockpit air contains insufficient oxygen pressure to support physiological requirements. At a cockpit altitude of 10,000 feet or below, pulling the GREEN RING is optional as ambient cockpit air contains sufficient oxygen pressure to support
physiological requirements.
N - When the emergency oxygen system is actuated, high pressure air may make verbal communication with the other crewmember or
ATC more difficult.
N - Once activated, ejection seat emergency oxygen cannot be shut off and will provide oxygen flow until the cylinder is depleted (10 minutes). Since the emergency oxygen system is not regulated, it is normal for pressure to gradually decrease to the point it feels like the oxygen is depleted before reaching 10
minutes of use, however oxygen is still being
supplied.
N - Sharply pull the green ring up and aft to activate the emergency oxygen system. Several up and aft pull attempts may be required to
fully activate oxygen flow.
N - Pull force to activate the emergency oxygen
system may be as high as 40 pounds.

(1C/1N)
N - If the FUEL PX warning remains illuminated, the engine-driven high pressure fuel pump is suction feeding. Engine operation with high pressure pump suction feeding is limited to 10 hours.
C - Unless a greater emergency exists, do not reset BOOST PUMP circuit breaker (left front console) if open.

(3W/1N)
W - To avoid injury, grasp handle and pull sharply toward abdomen, keeping elbows against the body.
W - The emergency escape system incorporates an explosive canopy fracturing system. The force of detonation blows numerous shards and small fragments outward from the canopy and into the cockpit. Some metallic fragments may be extremely hot and may cause burns upon contact with the skin. Aircrew should ensure exposed skin is covered, the oxygen mask is on, and visor is down prior to ejection or actuating the CFS system to prevent injury from shards and hot fragments.
W - When ejecting over mountainous terrain exceeding 8000 feet MSL, the manual override (MOR) handle should be used to manually separate from the seat and deploy the parachute.
N - If ejecting at low speed, one or both sets of risers may remain velcroed together following seat separation. This may create a slight increase in descent rate and/or an uncommanded turn. Manually separate the risers if time permits. The steering lines (toggles) are located on the backside of each of the front risers. To counter any uncommanded turns, unstow the opposite steering line or use risers
for controllability.

(1W)
W - After a stop which required maximum effort braking and if overheated brakes are suspected, do not taxi into or park in a congested area until brakes have had sufficient time to cool. Do not set parking brake.

(1W/1N)
W - Under varying conditions of fire and/or smoke where aircraft control is jeopardized, the pilot has the option of actuating CFS or
ejecting.
N - If a faulty component can be identified as the source of smoke and fumes, turn defective unit off or pull respective circuit breaker. Circuit breakers for items on the hot battery bus are not accessible in flight.

(4W)
W - Illumination of the fire warning light accompanied by one or more of the following indications is confirmation of an engine fire: smoke; flames; engine vibration; unusual sounds; high ITT; and fluctuating oil pressure,
oil temperature, or hydraulic pressure.
W - A fire warning light with no accompanying indication is not a confirmed fire. Do not shut down an engine for an unconfirmed fire.
W - High engine compartment temperatures resulting from a bleed air leak may cause illumination of the fire warning light. Reducing the PCL setting towards IDLE will decrease the amount of bleed air and possibly extinguish the fire warning light; however, advancing the PCL might be required to intercept the ELP. Regardless of reducing or advancing the PCL, continue to investigate
for indications confirming an engine fire.
W - If the fire cannot be confirmed, the fire warning system may be at fault and should be tested as conditions permit. If only one fire loop annunciator is illuminated (top or bottom half only), a false fire indication may
exist if the other loop tests good.

(3W/5N)
N - Zoom results with an engine still producing a usable torque (>6%) will be several hundred to several thousand feet higher in altitude
gained.
N - Each low altitude zoom capability chart depicted in Figure 3-2, Figure 3-3, and Figure 3-4 represents a no engine condition. Each chart assumes the pilot will not perform any action prior to actual engine failure.
N - If experiencing uncommanded power changes/loss of power/uncommanded propeller feather or compressor stalls, refer to
appropriate procedure.
N - Propeller will not feather unless the PCL is
fully in OFF.
W - If a suitable landing surface is available, turn immediately to intercept the nearest suitable point on the ELP. Any delay could result in insufficient gliding distance to reach a landing surface.
W - Do not delay decision to eject below 2000
feet AGL.
W - Airstart procedure is not recommended below 2000 feet AGL, as primary attention should be to eject or safely recover the aircraft.
N - Crosscheck N1 against other engine indications to assess condition of engine and determine if an airstart is warranted. At 125 KIAS, an engine which has flamed out will rotate below 8% N1 and indicate 0% N1. The engine oil pressure indicator may display oil pressures up to 4 psi with or without the engine seized.

(2W/2N)
W - If insufficient runway remains to land
straight ahead, consider immediate ejection.
W - Do not sacrifice aircraft control while troubleshooting or lowering gear with emergency system.
N - The pilot should select IDLE to use the increased drag of the not yet feathered propeller or select OFF to reduce the sink rate.
N - With a loss of hydraulic pressure, landing gear and flaps cannot be lowered by normal means.

flashcards.answer:
(5W/2C/4N)
W - Aircraft may float while approaching touchdown with the propeller feathered more than observed while conducting practice forced landing at 4-6% torque. Energy management is critical to achieving targeted touchdown position. Landing ground roll distance will increase with the propeller feathered.
W - Landing on an unprepared surface may cause structural damage making it impossible to open the canopy or fracture it using the CFS.
W - Engine failure or shutdown will completely disable the bleed air system. Depending on environmental conditions, this may cause significant canopy icing and/or fogging, and severely hamper visibility, especially from
the rear cockpit.
C - Ejection is recommended if a suitable landing area is not available. If circumstances dictate an emergency landing and ejection is not possible or the ejection system malfunctions, the pilot may perform an ELP to an unprepared
surface or ditch the aircraft. The aircraft structure can survive either type of forced landing; however, the risk of injury increases significantly due to crash loads and the complexity of ground or water egress.
C - Inducing yaw (side slipping) with a known engine/oil malfunction could result in impaired windshield visibility due to oil leakage
spraying onto the windshield.
W - If landing on an unprepared surface or ditching, do not extend the landing gear. Flaps will not be available without emergency gear
extension.
N - Normal safe indications with electrical power, when the emergency extension system has been used to lower the gear, are two green main gear lights, two red main door lights, green nose gear light, and red light in
handle.
W - Do not lower flaps LDG until landing is assured. Drag will increase dramatically once landing flaps are lowered.
N - Selecting either TO or LDG flaps will extend the flaps to the commanded position if the landing gear has been extended using the emergency extension system and if battery power is available.
N - Landing gear/flap retraction is not possible when the emergency extension system has been used.
N - Nose wheel steering is unavailable with an inoperative engine. Maintain directional control with rudder and differential braking.

(2W/3C/7N)
N - Mid range is a physical PCL angle that approximates the midway position between IDLE and MAX.
N - A PCL position above IDLE will provide the
best chance for the engine to recover.
N - A mid-range PCL position will minimize the potential of engine overtorque and/or overtemperature when the PMU is turned OFF.
C - There is a potential for ITT limits to be exceeded if the PMU switch is turned OFF with ITT ≥820 °C.
C - Ground idle will not be available during landing rollout and taxi. Plan for increased landing distances due to higher IDLE N1
(approximately 67%).
N - With constant airspeed and torque, RPM can be considered stable if below 40% and no upward change for a 3-second period.
N - If NP indicator is displaying red X’s, switching the PMU to NORM and back OFF will reset the PMU and should restore the NP indication.
N - Propeller should come out of feather within
15-20 seconds.
W - If rate of descent (indicated on the VSI while stabilized at 125 KIAS with gear, flaps, and speed brake retracted and 4-6% torque) is greater than 1500 ft/min, increase torque as necessary (up to 131%) to achieve approximately
1350-1500 ft/min rate of descent. If engine power is insufficient to produce a rate of descent less than 1500 ft/min, set PCL to
OFF.
N - The pilot should consider moving the PCL through the full range of motion to determine power available.
C - Consideration should be given to leaving the
engine operating with PCL at mid range.
W - With the PROP SYS circuit breaker pulled and the PMU switch OFF, the feather dump solenoid will not be powered. The propeller will feather at a slower rate as oil pressure decreases and the feathering spring takes effect. Glide performance will be considerably reduced and it may not be possible to
intercept or fly the emergency landing pattern.

flashcards.answer:
(1W/1N)
N - Setting the DEFOG switch to ON automatically selects high bleed air inflow and will alleviate back pressure on the engine compressor.
W - When the engine is so underpowered that high rates of descent occur, any delay in shutting down the engine to feather the propeller may result in insufficient altitude to reach a suitable landing site.

(2W/1C/1N)
W - Improperly positioning the control stick/elevator aft of the neutral position may significantly delay or prevent the aircraft from recovering from an OCF/spin which could result in loss of aircraft and/or crew.
N - Cycling of control positions or applying antispin controls prematurely can aggravate aircraft motion and significantly delay recovery.
W -
Recommended minimum altitude for ejection
is 6000 feet AGL.
C - Power-on and inverted departures or spins will result in high loads on the engine and torque shaft. If an inverted or power-on departure is encountered, land as soon as conditions permit. The pilot should suspect possible engine damage and may experience unusual engine operation accompanied by
low oil pressure or CHIP detector warning. In all cases of inverted or power-on departures, the engine shall be inspected by qualified
maintenance personnel after flight.

(4W/3C)
W - Airstart attempts outside of the airstart envelope may be unsuccessful or result in engine overtemperature. Consideration should be given to ensure airstarts are attempted within the airstart envelope (125-200 KIAS for sea level to 15,000 feet, or 135-200 KIAS for 15,001 to 20,000 feet).
W - Do not delay ejection while attempting airstart
at low altitude if below 2000 feet AGL.
W - PCL must be in OFF to feather the propeller, and ensure proper starter, ignition, boost pump, and PMU operation during airstart.
C - Ensure PCL is in OFF; otherwise, fuel may
be prematurely introduced during start.
C - Continuous operation with the BOOST PUMP switch in the ON position will cause damage to the engine-driven low pressure fuel pump. Upon landing, notify maintenance of the duration of flight with BOOST PUMP
switch in the ON position.
C - If N1 does not rise within 5 seconds, discontinue the airstart attempt and proceed to IF AIRSTART IS UNSUCCESSFUL due to
suspected mechanical failure.
W - Movement of the PCL above IDLE before N1 stabilizes at approximately 67% will cause an increase in fuel flow which may cause engine
failure due to a severe ITT overtemperature.
C - If there is no rise in ITT within 10 seconds after fuel flow indications, place the PCL to OFF and abort the start.

(5W/2N)
N - In a situation requiring immediate ground egress, the ejection system has the capability for 0/0 ejection.
W - Failure to ensure that the ISS mode selector is set to SOLO may result in the inadvertent ejection of one or both seats.
W - Failure to insert both ejection seat safety pins (if occupied) before ground egress may result in inadvertent activation of ejection sequence and subsequent injury or death when performing
emergency ground egress.
W - If the canopy fracturing system malfunctions in conjunction with a canopy latch failure in the locked position, ejection may be the only option remaining to exit the aircraft. Aircrew shall remove the ejection seat safety pin and ensure shoulder straps, lap straps, and leg restraint garters are still attached prior to pulling
ejection handle.
W - To prevent injury, ensure oxygen mask is on and visor is down prior to actuating the CFS system.
W - Each internal CFS handle activates only the CFS charge for the respective transparency. Both internal CFS handles must be activated in order to fracture both transparencies (if required).
N - Oxygen hose, emergency oxygen hose, communication leads, and anti-G suit hose will pull free while vacating cockpit and leg restraint lines will pull through leg restraint garter D rings if released with quick-release
lever.

(1W)
W - Higher power settings accompanied by high ITT may aggravate the existing condition. However, if ITT is within limits reducing power could result in engine flameout.

(2N)
N - note and report to MX the degree and duration of any overtemperature
N - If start is initiated with PCL in the OFF position, abort by reselecting AUTO/RESET on the STARTER switch. If start is initiated with PCL out of the OFF position, but not past the IDLE gate, abort by placing the PCL to OFF
or reselecting AUTO/RESET on the
STARTER switch. If the PCL is past the
IDLE gate, abort by placing the PCL to OFF.

(4W/2C)
W - If the engine should fail while flying the PEL, refer to the Engine Failure During Flight checklist, and transition to the Forced Landing
procedure.
W - If rate of descent (indicated on the VSI while stabilized at 125 KIAS with gear, flaps, and speed brake retracted and 4 to 6% torque) is greater than 1500 ft/min, increase torque as necessary (up to 131%) to achieve approximately 1350 to 1500 ft/min rate of descent. If engine power is insufficient to produce a rate of descent less than 1500 ft/min, set PCL to OFF.
W - Once on profile, if engine is vibrating excessively, or if indications of failure are imminent, set PCL to OFF.
W - Engine failure or shutdown will completely disable the bleed air system. Depending on environmental conditions, this may cause significant canopy icing and/or fogging, severely hampering visibility, especially
from the rear cockpit.
C - Inducing yaw (side slipping) with a known engine/oil malfunction could result in impaired windshield visibility due to oil leakage
spraying onto the windshield.
C - At higher temperature and pressure altitudes, power response will be delayed. Airspeeds below 110 KIAS on ELP final, in combination with transitioning to a high flare, may lead to a hard landing resulting in landing
gear component failure.

If N1 does not rise within 5 seconds, stop the attempt.
If ITT does not rise within 10 seconds after fuel flow, abort the start.
Do not advance the PCL above IDLE before N1 stabilizes around 67 percent.

items.text: Airstarts below 2000 feet AGL are usually a trap. Below that altitude, primary attention belongs on landing or ejecting.

sections.title: Engine Failure During Flight and Airstarts

items.text: Forced landing is used when the engine is inoperative or power is insufficient for continued flight.
The forced landing profile differs from a PEL because low energy is corrected by delaying drag, not by using power that no longer exists.

children.text: Minimum 120 KIAS until intercepting final and 110 KIAS on final.
Use emergency landing gear extension as required.
Transmit a distress call and configure the aircraft only as conditions permit.

items.text: Ejection is a life-saving action, not a failure, and it must be chosen before altitude and airspeed margins are gone.
The three ejection categories are immediate, time-critical, and controlled ejection.

children.text: Controlled ejection recommended above 2000 feet AGL.
Uncontrolled ejection recommended above 6000 feet AGL.
If the aircraft is no longer controllable, eject regardless of speed, altitude, or attitude.

items.text: The number one ejection failure is failure to pull the handle. Make the decision early.

studyNotes.summary: The decision chain is simple but unforgiving: recognize the failure, preserve energy, choose between restart, landing, or ejection, and do not waste the altitude you need for the next step.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion items

items.text: Crosswind takeoff and landing techniques are the same fundamentals from earlier events, but the expectation is now faster recognition and cleaner correction.
In the pattern, use crab on downwind and a wing-low final to stay aligned with the runway.
Wave off if more than 45 degrees of bank is required or if drift, crab, or side motion remain unresolved.
An abort is mandatory for abnormal or unsafe conditions before max abort speed, but aircraft control remains the priority.
Maximum braking requires a smooth, increasing application as speed decreases, with immediate release if directional control is lost.
If the aircraft departs or is about to depart the prepared surface, execute Emergency Engine Shutdown on the Ground and Emergency Ground Egress as required.
Do not request the barrier. If a raised barrier or runway excursion removes recovery margin, preserving life takes priority over preserving the aircraft.
Emergency Ground Egress still hinges on ISS SOLO, seat pins installed, parking brake as required, and canopy open if possible.
If the canopy cannot be opened, both cockpit CFS actions and strap release steps must be executed correctly before evacuation.
Once clear of the aircraft, move away at a 45-degree angle off the tail and remain alert for emergency vehicles.
Windshear planning includes adding margin where authorized, using takeoff flaps, and avoiding severe windshear or microburst environments when possible.
If windshear is encountered on approach, execute an immediate go-around or waveoff.
A UFCP failure limits normal cockpit access to some comm and nav functions, but the MFD NAV page provides the backup path needed to continue and land as soon as practical.

studyNotes.summary: The emphasis is on pattern discipline under bad conditions: stay aligned, respect braking limits, and know when an abnormal runway or cockpit condition demands an immediate waveoff, shutdown, or egress.

items.text: The AOA approach teaches precise energy and attitude control using optimum AOA instead of raw airspeed as the primary approach reference.

children.text: Transition to on-speed AOA on downwind after gear and flap configuration.
Maintain about 10.5 units AOA through the 180 and 90 positions.
Arrive near 450 feet AGL at the 90 and about 200 feet AGL on final.

items.text: The intent is an AOA approach to a normal flared landing, not an AOA arrival flown all the way onto the runway.
Contact unusual attitudes are visual recoveries from nose-high, nose-low, or inverted attitudes and must be completed above 6000 feet AGL.

children.text: Nose-high: use coordinated roll and positive G to recover, not forward stick.
Nose-low: roll to the nearest horizon, reduce power as required, and recover without overspeeding.
Inverted: roll the shortest way to the horizon and recover smoothly.

items.text: If stalled or in OCF, unusual-attitude recovery is no longer the right answer. Transition to the appropriate departure recovery or eject if altitude is gone.
Aileron Roll emphasizes correct entry airspeed, a brief pitch-up, back-stick relaxation, and a clean roll about the longitudinal axis.
Loop emphasizes a constant-heading vertical maneuver using about 4 Gs on entry, coordinated rudder, and disciplined pull management over the top.
Half Cuban Eight combines loop mechanics with a 45-degree nose-low rolling segment and requires good pitch-rate control before the roll.
For all aerobatics, complete the proper checklist, clear the area, and respect entry altitude, airspeed, and G limits.
Operating maneuvering speed is 227 KIAS, and full or abrupt control inputs above that speed can damage the aircraft.
Full rudder above 150 KIAS exceeds rudder-system limits even below VO.
Other key limits in this event include VMO, turbulence penetration speeds, and 150 KIAS flap or gear extension limits.

studyNotes.summary: The common thread is disciplined energy control. Whether you are flying an AOA pattern or an aerobatic figure, success depends on entering with the right setup and staying ahead of the attitude and airspeed picture.

items.text: IMSAFE stands for illness, medication, stress, alcohol, fatigue, and eating, and it is the first risk-management check in every brief.
If an SNA is not fit to fly, the process includes notifying the IP, going to the ODO, and completing the appropriate IMSAFE paperwork and medical referral if required.
IMSAFE is not a loophole for poor planning. It is a safety tool that applies to any syllabus event, not just flights.
CRM is the use of behavioral skills to reduce preventable crew error and optimize risk management.
Core ideas emphasized in this event include:
SNAs still need to perform as if single-piloted even when an IP is present. Good CRM does not replace aircraft control; it supports it.
See and avoid remains the primary defense against midair collisions, especially in VMC near airports.

children.text: Accommodation delay when shifting focus outside.
A narrow focus zone and blossom effect.
Reduced detection from haze, glare, or dirty windscreens.

items.text: This recovery only works well if you enter stabilized and stay ahead of the configuration timeline.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion items

items.text: The 3 C's are configuration, checklist, and clear area.
They are performed before stall-related maneuvers to ensure the aircraft is configured correctly, required checklists are complete, and the area is safe.
Clearing turns should be deliberate and flown in a way that supports the next maneuver rather than wastes time and airspace.
Slow flight trains control of the aircraft near stall speed in a configuration similar to takeoff and landing.

SCATSAFE demonstrates how the airplane behaves at high AOA through straight-and-level flight, coordination exercises, adverse yaw, torque effects, steep turns, abrupt inputs, flap retraction, and reduced control effectiveness.
Common themes in both maneuvers are smooth inputs, heavy trim use, ball control, and understanding that the airplane responds sluggishly at low energy.
Energy is altitude plus airspeed, and the best contact pilots manage both continuously instead of reacting after the fact.

children.text: About 1000 feet of altitude is roughly equivalent to 50 KIAS in the right conditions.
High power and low AOA build energy.
Drag, low power, and G-loading spend energy.

items.text: Useful rules from this event include:
Good energy management reduces the time wasted repositioning between maneuvers.
A slip is an intentional out-of-balance maneuver used to lose altitude while holding airspeed and ground track.
The core technique is lowering one wing while applying opposite rudder to keep the desired track.
Monitor descent rate, airspeed, and bank carefully. Recovery must begin early enough to arrest the descent without large or rough control inputs.

studyNotes.summary: Everything in this event gets better when the setup is clean. Clear the area, configure correctly, and then let airspeed, trim, and coordination tell you what the airplane is trying to do.

items.text: Goliad, Waldron, Aransas County, and Ingleside all require early communication, pattern-entry discipline, and awareness of who owns right-of-way.

If you lose contact, the entry is no longer routine. Execute the discontinued or lost-comm plan rather than pressing into an uncertain pattern.
Crosswind takeoff still means aileron into the wind, rudder to counter weathervaning, and reducing aileron as airspeed builds.
Crosswind landings use a wing-low method with the upwind wheel touching first and crosswind corrections held through rollout.
If side motion, drift, or crab remain at touchdown, the right answer is not to salvage it on the runway. The right answer is to wave off.

children.text: More than 45 degrees of bank on final.
Preceding aircraft not landed when you are on rollout.
Unstable energy, drift, or alignment that cannot be corrected without overcontrolling.

items.text: Fly the waveoff with wings level, ball centered, the right climb attitude, and the correct flap retraction timeline.

items.text: Know why military operating areas (moas) matters and be able to explain it simply: The FAA established MOAs in which certain military flight training may be conducted on a scheduled basis
Know why restricted area (r) matters and be able to explain it simply: Flights are prohibited during published periods of use unless permission is obtained from controlling authority
Know why warning area (w) matters and be able to explain it simply: Flights are not restricted but avoidance is advised during time of use
Know why alert area (a) matters and be able to explain it simply: Flights are not restricted. An area where there is concentrated student training or other unusual area activity of operator sig...
Know why actual directories (us, canada, and mexico matters and be able to explain it simply: Airport/Facilities Directory - US *must meet certain requirements defined in the Legend

questions.explanation: CNAF M-3710.7: flights shall not be made in IMC conditions within controlled airspace until an ATC clearance has been obtained
questions.prompt: (T/F) It is permissible to depart in IMC conditions from an uncontrolled airfield without an IFR clearance, so long as you have filed a flight plan and intend on receiving your IFR clearance once airborne.
(T/F) During taxi operations at unfamiliar fields, if available, the Airport Diagram should be open and accessible for reference.
(T/F) Readback of runway holding instructions in a taxi clearance is not required.

questions.explanation:
After rotating on an instrument TO, set nose attitude to approximately _____ to _____ degrees nose up until reaching _____ KIAS.
8; 10; 180
If the phraseology “Climb via SID” is included in the altitude portion of a flight clearance, the pilot is required to comply with published _____.
questions.prompt: (T/F) ATIS is 500 overcast and ¾ mile visibility. The only approach to the duty runway is a NPA with weather minimums of 400-¾ . This meets CNAF 3710 TO requirements for a standard instrument rated pilot.
(T/F) All SIDs will have a “Top Altitude.” Top Altitudes will always be assigned by ATC.

questions.answer: Refer to the TO Minimums section in the front of the FLIP Terminal Book
questions.explanation:
Unless specified otherwise, required obstacle clearance for all departures, including diverse, is based on _____.
Pilot crossing the departure end of the runway at least 35 feet above the departure end of runway elevation
Climbing to 400 feet above the departure end of runway elevation before making the initial turn
questions.prompt: (T/F) When a “Trouble T” is annotated on an IAP or DP the pilot should _____.

questions.explanation:
Route
Altitude
Frequency
questions.prompt: What items are normally included in an IFR flight clearance?
What additional piece of information is included in the IFR flight clearance, when departing IMC from a Non-Tower controlled field, and obtaining the clearance over the phone from a FSS?
What items are REQUIRED to be read back in a taxi clearance?
(T/F) With a standard instrument rating, CNAF 3710 requires that departure weather allow for an emergency return for the landing runway in use.

questions.explanation:
Associated speed restrictions
Associated altitude restrictions along the cleared route or procedure
questions.prompt: If the phraseology “Climb via SID” is included in the altitude portion of a flight clearance, the pilot is required to comply with which published items on the SIDs?

(T/F) When assigned to “Climb via SID”, the final expected level off altitude during the SID (after meeting any intermediate charted restrictions) without further clearance is referred to as a “Top Altitude”.

questions.explanation:
Unless specified otherwise, required obstacle clearance for ALL departures, including diverse, based on crossing the departure end of the runway at least _____ feet above the departure end of runway elevation, climbing to _____ feet above the departure end of runway elevation before making the initial turn, and maintaining a minimum climb gradient of _____ feet per NM.
35; 400; 200
Airports on an IFR Enroute Chart that are depicted _____ in color can always be found in the DOD FLIP Terminal High Altitude books.
questions.prompt: (T/F) “Top Altitudes” for a SID only exist when they are displayed in a box labeled “Top Altitude” in the planview section of a SID.

questions.explanation:
“Texan 123, you are cleared to HOLUP intersection, HARD ONE departure, climb via SID…” Based on this clearance, the clearance limit is _____. Upon arrival at that limit you are expected to _____ if no further instructions have been received.
HOLUP Intersection; enter holding as depicted (if published) or use STD pattern along arrival route of flight
questions.prompt: (T/F) Airports on an IFR Enroute Chart that are depicted in Green in color will always be published in the DOD FLIP Terminal Low Altitude books.

questions.answer: Set altimeter to the current reported altimeter setting of a station along the route and within 100 NM of the aircraft
questions.explanation: Air traffic controllers will furnish the setting to the pilot at least once while the aircraft is in the controllers’ area of jurisdiction
questions.prompt: What is true regarding altimeter settings for operations below 18,000’ MSL when local pressure is 31.00 inHG or less?

questions.answer: Reporting changes of altitude to maintain VMC are required
questions.explanation:
This does not imply cancellation of the IFR flight plan
Appropriate VFR altitudes shall be maintained
Minimum IFR altitudes must be complied with
questions.prompt: What is true regarding operating on an IFR flight plan and approved to operate “VFR ON-TOP”?

questions.explanation:
Inflight changes to route or destination can always be handled by the ATC facility controlling your aircraft.
False
questions.prompt: (T/F) A pilot on an IFR clearance has “Canceled IFR” and is proceeding VFR. Shortly afterwards, IFR handling is needed due to weather along the route. In this case the pilot may simply “Request resume IFR” with ATC to continue with the original IFR clearance.

questions.answer: Vacating any previously assigned altitude for a newly assigned altitude
questions.explanation:
Altitude changes when operating on a clearance specifying “VFR On Top”
Hazardous conditions which have not been forecast
questions.prompt: What are some reports that will be required without a specific ATC request?

questions.explanation:
Maintain VMC and continue under VFR. Land as soon as practical and notify ATC.
Within 51 NM of  NAVAID the width of an airway’s primary obstacle clearance area is _____.
A protected width of 8 NM with 4 NM on each side of the centerline
questions.prompt: (T/F) If you have lost comms and are in VMC conditions, you are required to land at the nearest suitable airport.
(T/F) During airways navigation, turns required at a NAVAID should always employ the FTI Over-The-Station Intercept (OSI) procedures.
(T/F) When coordinating with FSS to change your destination or route of flight, a simple DRAFT report will suffice for all the information they require.

questions.answer: All compulsory reporting points are required unless ATC instructs otherwise
questions.explanation:
Once you have concluded that lost communications cannot be restored, the transponder should be set to 7600, and if continuing IFR, the altitude should be _____.
The highest of:
Your assigned altitude
questions.prompt: When an ATC controller advises you “Radar services terminated”, what is true concerning an IFR flight plan?
(T/F) the IAF for an approach will never be located as a fix, waypoint, or NAVAID along the enroute structure.
(T/F) During a Radar Arrival, ATC will provide heading and altitude instructions. Their altitude assignments will never be lower than those noted on your chart or approach plates.

questions.answer: Once the aircraft has vacated an altitude, it may not return to that altitude
questions.prompt: When ATC clears a pilot to descend “At Pilot’s Discretion”, what action is the pilot not allowed to execute?

questions.explanation:
Approaching 220 KIAS set power to 10% torque
Fine tune power and nose
*10/10/220 rule
questions.prompt: To begin a typical enroute descent when cruise speed is less than 220 KIAS, the FTI recommends what actions to meet the charted NATOPS enroute descent profile?

questions.explanation:
You need to lose 8000’ in 8 NM. Based on a GS of 240 knots, that will require a rate of descent of _____. (reference rate of climb/descent table)
4000 fpm
While enroute at FL 250, favorable winds are affording a nice 30 knots GS. You need to lose 10,000’ to meet a crossing altitude restriction at your next fix. For descent planning purposes, to maintain the 300 knots GS with a gentle 2000 fpm descent rate, you should begin your descent no later than ____ NM from the fix. (reference rate of climb/descent table)
questions.prompt: (T/F) The ABCD checklist must be accomplished in order.

(T/F) Obtaining ATIS 100 NM from the destination will ensure you have an appropriate altimeter setting for the terminal area. Getting this “A” step of the ABCDs out of the way early relieves you of checking ATIS later.

questions.explanation:
Weather minimums
NAVAID setup
IAF
questions.prompt: What are the items included in the FTI Instrument Approach Brief?

questions.explanation:
VHF Com2
VHF Nav
The Instrument FTI calls for the descent checklist to be accomplished _____.
questions.prompt: You may be unable to completely setup your cockpit until actually commencing the approach. What items can be preloaded in standby without changing your current settings?

questions.explanation:
Intermediate Approach
Final Approach
Missed Approach
questions.prompt: (T/F) Each IAP may be divided into as many as 4 segments:

questions.explanation:
During execution of the HILO IAP, multiple orbits needed to dissipate altitude or airspeed are allowed at pilots’ discretion.
False
Some situations may require faster than normal cruise along the arcing portion of an approach. However, the FTI Arcing Approach Procedures normally call for transition to slow cruise _____.
questions.prompt: (T/F) All low altitude PT approaches have a published FAF.

questions.answer: You are cleared to an IAF with a published PT or HILO procedure
questions.explanation:
During a HILO approach, at the completion of the outbound leg, turn inbound and always use a DAI to establish the aircraft on the inbound course prior to crossing the holding fix.
False
During the Teardrop Approach, after _____ minute(s) of outbound timing, turn inbound and set a _____ intercept if not within _____ of the inbound course.
questions.prompt: During an instrument approach, published course reversals are mandatory for what situations?

questions.answer: You can descend to the altitude depicted on the feeder route
questions.prompt: What altitudes can you descend to if you are using a feeder facility and are cleared for the approach?

questions.explanation:
During a SI Approach, if the distance from the IAF to the FAF is more than _____ NM, normal cruise airspeed should be maintained until _____ NM from the FAF before slowing to 150 KIAS.
10; 10
questions.prompt: (T/F) A Straight-In Approach is an IAP conducted by navigating from an IAF to establish the aircraft on the intermediate or final approach segment via a direct final path. This type of approach must be completed using the Straight-In Landing Minimums for that approach.

questions.explanation:
Feeder Routes
IAFs collocated in the enroute structure
Terminal Arrival Areas
questions.prompt: What common methods are used to transition from the Enroute structure into a Terminal area?

questions.answer: Alphabetically by STAR name (not by airfield)
questions.prompt: How are STARs listed in the Standard Terminal Arrival Publication?

questions.answer: Pilot must maintain last assigned altitude until receiving authorization to descend
questions.prompt: During a STAR, when instructed “Cleared (STAR name) Arrival” are you required to comply with altitude restrictions published on the STAR?
During a STAR, when instructed “Descend via (STAR name) Arrival”, what is the pilot authorized to do?

questions.answer: AC in position to expect clearance or be vectored for an approach
questions.prompt: STARs are designed to terminate at what point?

questions.answer: Applicable approach plates; thick lined arrows
questions.prompt: Where feasible, IAFs are collocated with NAVAIDS, waypoints, or intersections along the enroute structure. Where and how are they depicted?

questions.answer: Based on the magnetic bearing of the AC TO the fix labeled IF/IAF
questions.prompt: When using an approach that has published TAAs, ATC expects the pilot to use an appropriate IAF based on which TAA will be entered. How does a pilot determine which TAA sector and IAF is applicable for their arrival?
When may the altitudes in a TAA sector be used?
When an airway does not cross the lateral TAA boundaries, what may be depicted in the enroute structure?

questions.explanation:
ATC less concerned with speed or rate of descent.
Pilots optimize for fuel efficiency or ground speed.
Terminal Descents:
questions.prompt: How do descents in the terminal area differ from those conducted in the enroute structure?

As 200 KIAS is the most common airspeed used for terminal descents in the T-6B, what Power and Attitude setting is used to maintain this common speed during the descent? What approximate rate of descent will those settings provide?

questions.answer: ATIS, Brief, Cockpit Setup, Descent Checklist
questions.prompt: The acronym ABCD is a mnemonic that can aid in arrival planning. What does it stand for?

questions.answer: Approach name, Wx mins, NAVAID setup, IAF, Course(s), Segment altitudes, MDA/DA, MAP, Missed approach/Climb-out instructions, Unusual or noteworthy items peculiar to the approach
questions.prompt: What items are contained in the FTI instrument approach Brief?

questions.explanation:
Intermediate Approach
Final Approach
Missed Approach

questions.answer: Where the published GS/GP intercepts the minimum GS/GP intercept altitude shown on the chart

questions.answer: Designated FAF, depicted by Maltese Cross or
questions.explanation: Point where the AC is established inbound on the final approach course
questions.prompt: How is the FAF determined on a non-precision approach?

questions.answer: Precision: occurs at the DA or DH on the GS/GP
questions.explanation: NP: fix, waypoint, NAVAID, or after specific elapsed time after crossing the FAF
questions.prompt: How is the location of the MAP determined during precision and non-precision approaches?

With the exception of Radar Vectored approaches and some Straight-In approaches, when do you normally transition from cruise speed to 150 KIAS? What power setting is typically used to effect this transition?

questions.answer: 5 NM prior to the FAF or upon reaching the FAP; 15% TQ, <150 KIAS, Gear down, Flaps TO, ~120 KIAS - 42% TQ, Before Landing Checklist
questions.prompt: With the exception of Radar Vectored approaches, when does the transition to BAC typically occur? How is the BAC transition typically conducted?

questions.answer: Pitch for airspeed, power for rate of descent not to exceed 1000 fpm
questions.prompt: During descents on the Final Approach Segment of any approach, FAA recommends maintaining a “Stabilized Approach”. What does the Instrument FTI direct in order to comply with this intent?

questions.answer: On or toward the maneuvering side
questions.prompt: During a procedure turn approach, you must complete all outbound maneuvering, to include the course reversal in what area?

questions.explanation:
Straight-In approach
NoPT routing
Established: holding pattern, cleared for the approach
questions.prompt: When are published course reversals not expected or required by ATC?
What types of navigational guidance may be used to define a Procedure track?

questions.explanation:
Enables aircraft to transition from the Initial Approach Fix (IAF) to the intermediate or final approach segment via a direct, straight path.
Avoids the need for course reversals like procedure turns or holding patterns.
No

questions.answer: IAF aligned with FAC, IAF not aligned with FAC
questions.prompt: What are two basic types of St-In approaches?

questions.answer: GPS waypoints, VHF intersections, DME fixes, NAVAIDS, Airports

questions.explanation:
Terminal (TERM) - 0.5 NM/Dot, 1 NM/full scale
Approach (APR) - 0.15 NM/Dot, 0.3 NM/full scale

questions.explanation:

questions.prompt: During a normal flight the FMS modes change automatically. When do these changes occur?

questions.answer: An imaginary point 1 NM outside the FAF, but no closer than 5 NM from runway.
questions.explanation: ATC aims to vector aircraft to intercept at least 2 NM outside this gate.
questions.prompt: What and where is the “Approach Gate” and how is it used by ATC when providing RVFAC?

questions.explanation:
Base: 150 KIAS
Extended straight/dog-leg: 200 KIAS until 15 NM from airport
questions.prompt: What are the FTI speeds used during RVFAC?

questions.explanation:
Maintain headings/altitudes until "cleared for approach" or “intercept and track inbound”
Turns onto FAC after clearance are pilot’s responsibility
Once established on final: comply with published courses/altitudes
questions.prompt: What are the pilot’s responsibilities concerning headings and altitudes during RVFAC?
(T/F) In the event of a “Full Scale” deflection of the CDI between the FAF and DA or MAP, the pilot should immediately re-intercept the FAC and continue descent to the DA or MDA.

questions.answer: VDPs generally provide an approximate glidepath of 3°
questions.explanation:
The pilot should not descend below the MDA prior to reaching a published VDP
The VDP will be identified by DME or RNAV along-track distance to the MAP
questions.prompt: What are some aspects concerning a published Visual Descent Point (VDP)?

questions.answer: It is identified by a Maltese cross in the profile view
questions.explanation:
It may occur over a VOR
It may occur at a specified VOR radial/DME
questions.prompt: What aspects are true concerning the FAF for a VOR approach?

questions.answer: Station Passage, Timing, DME, DME backed up by Timing
questions.prompt: What methods may be used to identify the MAP for a VOR approach?
(T/F) All named fixes on an IAP that occur between the FAWP and the MAWP will be included in the GPS database and shown during the approach.
(T/F) the 6 T’s are not required at the FAF during a GPS approach.

questions.explanation:
During the final approach segment, in order to maintain a “Stabilized Approach” the FTI directs power to be adjusted to maintain _____.
A stabilized rate of descent not to exceed 1000 fpm
questions.prompt: (T/F) During a Localizer Back Course (BC) approach, the aircraft will cross the localizer antenna prior to reaching the approach end of the runway.

questions.explanation:
PFD source LOC: +/- 2.5 degrees
PFD source FMS: +/- 0.3 NM
questions.prompt: What is true concerning CDI scale and sensitivity in the T-6B?

questions.explanation:
Pilot should not descend below the MDA prior to reaching a published VDP
Identified by DME or RNAV along-track distance to the MAP
Timing when used as the primary or backup means of identifying the MAP is based on _____.
questions.prompt: What is true concerning a Visual Descent Point (VDP)?

questions.answer: MISS APR on the NAV display
questions.explanation:
NPA on the NAV and PFD display
APR mode on the PFD display
During a GPS approach, segment altitudes and unnamed fixes such as a VDPs may not be coded into the waypoint sequence of the nav database. They must be identified by noting _____.
questions.prompt: During a GPS approach, within 2 NM of the FAWP what must be displayed to indicate suitable approach integrity?

questions.explanation:
During an ILS approach the precision FAF is _____.
The point where the GS intersects the published GS intercept altitude
Depicted in the profile view with a lightning bolt
questions.prompt: (T/F) The MAWP for a GPS approach will always be identified as RW##. The ## will represent the runway number such as RW21.

questions.answer: The intersection of two radials from two separate VHF Nav stations
questions.explanation:
During the _____ approach, the controller utilizes an airport surveillance radar system to transition the aircraft to final and then hands off to a PAR final controller. This “Final Controller” utilizes only the azimuth portion of the precision radar system.
PAR w/o GPS
questions.prompt: The localizer (non-precision) FAF will occur at the depicted Maltese Cross. Which method may not be used to identify this point in the T-6B?

questions.explanation:
During a PAR Approach, begin the descent to the DH _____.
When the controller advises “on glidepath”
During a PAR, arrival at the DH is primarily determined _____.
questions.prompt: (T/F) During a radar approach, transition to BAC and complete landing checks when established on final or dogleg to final and within 15 miles of the airport.

questions.explanation:
A No-Gyro Approach refers to an approach made without use of the _____.
Directional Gyro
During final on a PAR approach the controller will provide _____.
questions.prompt: (T/F) Other than different minimums and different radar systems used, the ASR and PAR w/o GS use the same concepts and procedures.

questions.answer: Add power and raise the nose slightly
questions.prompt: During a descent on a PAR the controller reports “going slightly below glidepath”. Currently, your airspeed is steady at 120 knots. What actions is/are needed to correct back to glidepath?

questions.answer: Execute missed approach or climb-out instructions
questions.prompt: What actions should be taken upon reaching the DH/DA during a PAR approach if the runway environment is not in sight?

questions.explanation:
When utilizing recommended altitudes, set power to approximately _____% torque, trim for 120 KIAS descent. Adjust rate of descent as required to meet recommended altitudes. It is your responsibility to reach MDA prior to the MAP.
24
During an ASR approach, upon reaching the published MDA if the runway is not in sight the pilot should _____.
questions.prompt: (T/F) During a PAR w/o GS or ASR approach the pilot may request recommended altitudes for final. These altitudes will be issued at each mile, based on the descent gradient established for the procedure, down to the last mile that is at or above the MDA. The stabilized descent they provide can help prevent loss of radar contact on final during heavy rain conditions.

questions.explanation:
In accordance with the T-6B Instrument FTI, during the penetration portion of a High Altitude IAP, power will be ____ and airspeed _____.
As required; 200-250 KIAS
The T-6B NATOPS Enroute Descent profile provides for 220 KIAS, 4000 fpm and approximately _____ feet of altitude loss for each NM traveled.
questions.prompt: (T/F) During the No-Gyro approach, turn immediately when directed using SRT (not to exceed 30° AOB) until on final, then make all turns at ½ SRT unless otherwise directed/

questions.explanation:
Higher TAS
Low altitude weather avoidance
questions.prompt: What is/are a(n) advantage(s) of using a high altitude instrument approach procedure?

questions.explanation:
Straight-In
Arcing
questions.prompt: What are types of procedure tracks used for high altitude instrument approach procedures?
(T/F) A penetration approach has an IAF altitude of FL280 at 29 DME. Its next segment has a hard altitude of 9000’ by 15 DME. A NATOPS enroute descent will not be sufficient to meet this requirement.
What approach category is used for the T-6B during a high altitude instrument approach procedure?
During a high altitude teardrop approach, if no turn DME or turn altitude is depicted in the profile view, at what point should you commence the inbound turn?

questions.explanation:
When a penetration completion altitude is depicted on a high altitude teardrop approach, do not descend below this altitude until you are established on the inbound segment of the approach. Established on course is defined as being within _____ radials of the FAC.
5
questions.prompt: (T/F) During a high altitude teardrop approach, after station passage at the IAF, begin descent when you are established on a parallel or intercept heading to the outbound course.
(T/F) When flying a Straight-In high altitude approach, you must overfly the IAF in all cases.
(T/F) During a high altitude arcing approach, plan all turns at standard rate.

questions.answer: Once the lead point is reached and a turn to the next approach segment is initiated
questions.explanation:
When transitioning from instruments (primary flight display) to visual references, look for the landing environment ____.
In the direction determined by relationship of the final course vector and visual references identified in the airport sketch
questions.prompt: During a high altitude arcing approach and turning onto or off of the arc, when may you begin descent to the next applicable altitude restriction?
(T/F) Bright approach lights suddenly appearing on final approach can give an impression of being below glidepath.

questions.explanation:
A sidestep maneuver is a procedure in which you fly a published instrument approach to one runway then perform _____ transition to land on an alternate runway.
A visual
When executing a missed approach, after placing the PCL to MAX, set the nose attitude to _____.
questions.prompt: (T/F) Flying an approach to a narrow runway may give the impression of being below glidepath on final.

questions.explanation:
The circling area is technically defined by the tangential connection of arcs drawn at the circling radius distance from each runway end. _____ feet of obstacle clearance is only ensured when maintaining the appropriate _____ within the circling radius.
300; MDA
Execute a missed approach during a circling maneuver if you _____.
questions.prompt: (T/F) If the runway environment becomes in sight after the VDP and prior to the MAP, there will always be sufficient runway available for a stabilized descent to touchdown.

questions.answer: When the aircraft is in a position to place the aircraft on a normal glidepath to the landing runway
questions.prompt: During a circling maneuver, when may the pilot descend below the published circling MDA?

questions.explanation:
During a missed approach the crucial priorities are _____.
Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Following a missed approach, when requesting clearance to an alternate airport it is recommended to use the DRAFT format. In this mnemonic the “T” stands for _____.
questions.prompt: (T/F) The sidestep maneuver is authorized for any approach with published circling minimums.

(T/F) If a missed approach is initiated during a circling or sidestep maneuver, initiate a turn in the last known direction of the landing runway as soon as the climb is established. Continue the turn until established on the missed approach procedure for the intended landing runway (assuming no climbout instructions were given)

questions.prompt: What is the primary method for obtaining flight route weather briefings?

questions.explanation:
The main purpose of any checkpoint is to _____.
Provide a verification of the accuracy of your preflight planning
As a general rule of thumb, checkpoints should be between _____ and _____ minutes apart.
questions.prompt: (T/F) NOTAMS contained in the Notice to Airmen Publication (NTAP) will not be included by an FSS brief unless specifically requested by the pilot.

questions.explanation:
Stop each course line at the edge of the checkpoint circles to preclude obscuring important data
The objective when creating your map is to give yourself points in time to cross-check position and validate planning. The best way to accomplish that is to plan the flight for a _____.
Constant groundspeed
questions.prompt: (T/F) When plotting courses on your VFR chart, the course line should extend inside the circle that highlights each checkpoint.

questions.explanation:
To convert your true course to a magnetic variation you _____ easterly variation.
Subtract
Magnetic Heading (MH) is Magnetic Course (MC) adjusted for _____.
questions.prompt: (T/F) Aircraft heading systems and aeronautical charts are both based on true north and south.

questions.explanation:
For VFR departures from civil “tower controlled” fields, clearance delivery _____.
Provides nothing and you are not required to call them for a VFR flight plan
questions.prompt: (T/F) A route study is a detailed examination of the planned flight concentrating on visualizing what you should see as you navigate the route.

questions.answer: Tower will activate your flight plan from a military field, FSS will activate your flight plan once airborne from a civilian field
questions.prompt: How is your flight plan activated when departing a military or civilian airfield?

questions.explanation:
If you do not have flight following and must change your VFR flight plan to IFR, you should first contact _____.
FSS and file a flight plan
If you change your VFR flight plan to an IFR flight plan with ATC, you need to contact FSS because _____.
questions.prompt: (T/F) While under flight following you can expect radar vectors to your route destination.
What are parts of DR navigation?

questions.explanation:
One method to use in measuring distance is used cockpit view angles. Another method discussed was _____.
Measuring the distance between two checkpoints on the chart
questions.prompt: (T/F) If you not see your checkpoint at the time you planned, you would turn to your next checkpoint based on time.

questions.explanation:
Using the proportional method to correct for time, you add/reduce _____ knots for every _____ second(s) late or early and hold this new airspeed for the number of minutes equal to your GS in mi/min.
1:1
questions.prompt: How long do you hold your correction using SCA if you are 1 mile left of your course?
You are going 3 NM/min and are 15 seconds early. How would you correct?
You are doing 4 mi/min and are 30 seconds late. How would you correct?
Your GS is 4 mi/min and you are 10 seconds late. What is your connection?

questions.explanation:
When departing VFR you should tell tower your _____.
Initial altitude and direction of flight
questions.prompt: What items would you record on the Jet Flight Log?

questions.answer: If your arrival time is going to change by more than 30 minutes
questions.prompt: When are you required to change your ETA on a VFR flight plan?
You are navigating at night using DR nav and approaching a checkpoint that you can’t see. When would you turn to the next checkpoint?
What are the primary scan positions on a VFR/low level nav route?
You are level at 3000’ AGL and, as you identify your checkpoint, you notice that you are off course. How far are you from the checkpoint, using wingtip references?

questions.explanation:
When checking if an airfield is OBO or requires a PPR, you should consult NOTAMS and _____.
The Enroute Supplement
questions.prompt: What is a course correction method that involves timing with a heading change?

questions.explanation:
When measuring a course, the key first step is to _____.
Determine the general direction of the course line
To convert your true course to magnetic course you _____ westerly variation.
questions.prompt: What are some examples of SUAs?

questions.explanation:
The main objective when completing the VFR map is to present all the essential information while _____.
Minimizing clutter and the amount of map detail obscured by the markings
If you have any questions or difficulties completing  military VFR flight plan, you should refer to _____ for guidance.
questions.prompt: On a VFR flight above 3000’ AGL and heading 090, what would be a legal altitude to maintain?
What are the 5 C’s?

questions.answer: Check your clock, fuel, and heading
questions.explanation:
When lost min-flight in overcast conditions, it is best to _____.
Climb to increase radio reception, but maintain VMC conditions
questions.prompt: What is the first thing you should do when you realize you are lost?

questions.answer: Climb in your area to increase visibility and radio reception, but stay below clouds and maintain VMC (17000’)
questions.explanation:
One way an FSS could help you when lost is by _____.
Providing weather information
If lost in-flight, set your transponder to _____.
questions.prompt: You are flying along in your training area at 13000’ and you become disoriented. Your instruments are not functioning properly, and there is a cloud deck at 17000’, what should you do?

questions.explanation:
Look for mandatory radar services if they are established at the destination airfield
Before you cancel your IFR flight plan and begin your VFR arrival you must first be _____.
In VFR condition and outside Class A Airspace
questions.prompt: Other than on the Sectional chart, where can you find information on a TRSA?

questions.answer: It has an operating tower and has a radar approach control
questions.prompt: Why is Pensacola classified as Class C airspace?

questions.answer: Callsign, position, altitude, transponder, and intentions
questions.explanation:
Also announce you have the current ATIS information by using the letter designator from the recording
Even though you might not use the OLS for your arrival, you should be aware of its presence on the field because _____.
It could present an obstruction hazard
questions.prompt: At minimum, what information should you provide at initial radio check-in when entering Class C airspace VFR?

questions.answer: Troubleshoot your radio connection and settings
questions.prompt: While maintaining aircraft control and continuing to clear, what is the first thing you should do after realizing you might have radio failure?

questions.explanation: If ATC is transmitting on the VOR, they might ask you to IDENT to acknowledge
questions.prompt: In a lost comm situation, how should you acknowledge the tower’s instructions?

questions.explanation:
If you learn there is a turbine-powered aircraft in the pattern it should be at _____ feet AGL.
1500
However, the pattern altitude could be 800’ AGL so you’ll need to exercise caution
questions.prompt: How is Class D airspace identified on VFR Sectional Charts?

questions.explanation: Be prepared to talk directly with other aircraft in the pattern
questions.prompt: What are two methods for communicating at an uncontrolled airfield?

questions.answer: They are located on the airfield to afford maximum visibility to pilots
questions.explanation:
It can be lighted for night operations
The landing strip indicators portray the _____.
Runway alignment
questions.prompt: What is true about the segmented circle?

questions.answer: Callsign, position, altitude, transponder code, and intentions
questions.explanation:
The _____ is a Navy-unique visual landing system providing glideslope information.
Optical Landing System (OLS)
The lateral dimensions of Class D airspace are normally _____.
questions.prompt: What information should you provide during initial radio contact when arriving VFR at a military airfield?

questions.answer: It reverts to Class E and is an uncontrolled airfield
questions.prompt: What happens if the tower at an airport in Class D airspace closes?

questions.explanation:
Two-way radio contact is not required when entering Class _____ airspace described with a shaded magenta line.
E
questions.prompt: What must occur prior to entering any Class D airspace to conduct a VFR arrival?

questions.answer: The tower is closed or operating part time, and there is no FSS
questions.explanation: You will usually use the CTAF or 122.9 VHF
questions.prompt: When should you use self-announce procedures during a VFR arrival to an unfamiliar field?

questions.answer: Basic, TRSA, Class B, and Class C
questions.prompt: The national terminal radar program provides which of the following services?

questions.answer: The aircraft with the lower altitude
questions.explanation: Try not to overtake it if you’re faster
questions.prompt: When approaching an uncontrolled, unfamiliar field VFR, who has the right of way for landing?
What is the first thing you should do after lost comm has been determined and you have checked your equipment?

questions.answer: Any airfield other than your home field
questions.prompt: What is the best definition of a strange field?

questions.explanation:
Engine oil should be checked within _____ minutes of shutdown.
30
A strange field preflight inspection should be completed _____.
questions.prompt: Who is responsible for making sure all postflight inspections are complete when at a strange field?

questions.explanation:
If you need assistance taxiing at a strange field, you can use  _____.
A follow-me truck
Progressive taxi instructions
questions.prompt: (T/F) Zero Fuel Weight (ZFW) of the aircraft includes the weight of the crew and baggage.

questions.answer: Call your home field SOF or FDO/ODO for guidance
questions.explanation:
Who normally closes your flight path at tower controlled fields.
Tower
questions.prompt: What should you do if you find a maintenance discrepancy while at a strange field?

questions.explanation:
At a military airfield you will fil your flight plan through _____, and at a civilian airfield you will file your flight plan through _____.
Base ops, FSS
During the preflight inspection, if the hydraulic reservoir fluid level indicator shows in the green area labeled _____ or _____, the system is fully serviced.
questions.prompt: What is the phone number for FSS?

questions.answer: To pass along your departure time
questions.prompt: When departing from a civilian field on an IFR flight plan, why should you call FSS after takeoff?

questions.answer: At the squadron operations desk or as locally designated
questions.prompt: Where do you find the aircraft’s Basic Empty Weight (BEW) for CG computations?
What is the best method to manage aircraft weigh in order to keep the CG within limits?
